Thirty comments

I’m really surprised this tune had not been posted here yet.
Donald Blue is a lovely Shetland Reel (traditional, I think). According to my teacher, it was named after the man called Donald Beu.

Michael McGoldrick and John McSherry recorded a slightly different version.

↳ Posted by slainte on December 2nd, 2002.

Combination

This tune gets along with O’ost Be Est Da Vong, another Shetland Reel. And also it is a good idea to play this tune before polkas.

↳ Posted by slainte on December 2nd, 2002.

Donald blue

This fantastic tune is actually a song, sng by the folk king’s Cappercaile.

↳ Posted by weemanwatson on February 22nd, 2003.

The best version I’ve heard of this tune is on John Creaven’s album. Check it out at Cdbaby.com, great flute player.

↳ Posted by Johnnie with the Queer Thing on December 29th, 2004.

This tune is also on “kitty lie over” with Mick O’Brian and Caoimhín O Raghallaigh. They play it after the hornpipe An Londubh (track 11), but they don’t list the name. It’s one of my favorite tunes off this recording.

↳ Posted by fiddleK on January 29th, 2005.

Donald Blue

At our session this tune is played in more of an Irish style and the B-part becomes more like Rolling In The Ryegrass. My personal preference is for the original Shetland setting that Yamadasan posted. I like it for its swingy simplicity.

Re: Donald Blue

This tune appears on Drop the Floor’s latest album ‘Fairly Cookin’ - following an adapted version of David Francie’s ’Annies House. I can’t comment on other versions or settings of the tune but, as far as I’m concerned, it continues to have resonance and will, I suspect, also continue to feature to in many Trad repertoires for a long time to come.
The DTF version is worth a listen though I confess to being 100% biased about this album as anyone checking it out will see! What I have learnt from this site is that there is a song to the tune too - so that is my next project.

Listen and enjoy - or complain!

↳ Posted by Steve Burke on October 21st, 2018.

Re: Donald Blue

No*.
Andy Linton’s quote above from 7 years ago :
“Traditional. As played by Fraser Hughson. Transcribed by Tom Anderson”
- comes from the Shetland fiddle collection “Da Mirrie Dancers”, printed in 1970.
* I can’t help but wonder - with reference to the previous post - if the “folk process” has come into play here, as “Donald Blue” is very often preceded by another well-known Shetland reel, “Jack Broke Da Prison Door.” Seems possible, the similarity in titles would suggest so.
To the best of my knowledge, this , undoubtedly a traditional Shetland reel, entered the Irish tradition through the playing of John “Watt” Henry, as it seems to have been associated with his name in the earliest Irish recordings of the tune.

↳ Posted by Kenny on May 21st, 2026.

Re: Donald Blue

I don’t see why this couldn’t be of Irish origin, if the earliest Shetland setting is from 1977; Johnny Watt was born 104 years ago, after all. Maybe Cathal McConnell learned it as a no namer from Johnny and passed it along to Aly Bain.

↳ Posted by What's the name of this tune? on May 29th, 2026.

Re: Donald Blue

Except the earliest Shetland setting isn’t from 1977.
As Kenny says above it appeared in “Da Mirrie Dancers”, published in 1970 and, even before that, according to the Traditional Tune Archive, it appeared in “Traditional Dancing in Scotland” by Flett & Flett from 1964.
Also according to the TTA, it was collected by Pat Shuldham Shaw (1917-1977). In “Hand Me Doon Ma Fiddle” Tom Anderson says the tune comes from Papa Stour, where it was called Donald Beu, after a teacher of the same name.

↳ Posted by DonaldK on May 29th, 2026.

Re: Donald Blue

There is no existing evidence anywhere I know of, that “Donald Blue” is anything other than a reel originating in Shetland.
